summary: Nehemiah, cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes in Susa, receives news of Jerusalem's precarious situation and obtains permission to rebuild the city's walls. Despite the opposition of Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem, the work is completed in fifty-two days. The book also narrates the public reading of the law by Ezra, the people's confession and the commitment signed by the community, the repopulation of Jerusalem and the dedication of the walls. It ends with Nehemiah's reforms in a second term as governor: the Sabbath, the tithes, the temple service and marriages with foreigners.
name: The book bears the name of Nehemiah, who speaks in the first person in much of the text; the name means “the LORD comforts.” In Hebrew tradition, Ezra and Nehemiah formed a single book; the Septuagint includes Nehemiah in Esdras B, and the Vulgate called it 2 Esdras. The separation into two books, common in Christian Bibles, was adopted later in printed Hebrew editions.
facts: 16th book of the Bible, among the historical books; in the Hebrew Bible, the second part of the book of Ezra–Nehemiah, among the Writings (Ketuvim)
historical narrative, largely first-person memoirs, with lists

structure.title: The final reforms
structure.text: On his return to Jerusalem, Nehemiah corrects abuses in the temple, on the Sabbath and in marriages.

extra.title: The memoirs of Nehemiah
extra.text: A large part of the book (especially 1–7 and 12:31–13:31) is written in the first person and has the tone of a personal account. In it appear short prayers in which Nehemiah asks God to remember him “with favor” (5:19; 13:14, 22, 31) or to remember the deeds of his adversaries (4:4–5; 6:14; 13:29). Many historians consider these memoirs one of the most direct sources on Judah in the Persian period.

writing.tradition: In Jewish tradition, Ezra and Nehemiah formed a single book, attributed to Ezra by the Babylonian Talmud (Bava Batra 15a); the first-person passages have been read as written by Nehemiah himself. On this reading, the book would date from the end of the 5th century BC, around 430–400 BC.
writing.academic: For most scholars, Nehemiah's memoirs are an authentic text, written by him around 430 BC, perhaps as an accounting of his work or as a votive inscription. A compiler joined them to the material about Ezra and to lists (the one in 7:6–73 repeats that of Ezra 2). The list in 12:10–11, 22 reaches the high priest Jaddua, whom the historian Josephus places in the time of Alexander the Great; for this reason the final form is usually dated c. 400–300 BC, although some identify Jaddua with an earlier priest. The chronological relationship between Ezra and Nehemiah, who appear together in 8:9 and 12:26, 36, is also debated.

events.intro: Nehemiah receives the news about Jerusalem in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes (1:1; 2:1), which corresponds to 445/444 BC, under Artaxerxes I. The wall is completed in fifty-two days (6:15), and Nehemiah governs Judah for twelve years, until the king's thirty-second year, c. 433 BC (5:14); he then returns to the court and comes back to Jerusalem some years later (13:6–7). Aramaic papyri from Elephantine, in Egypt, dated to 407 BC, mention the sons of Sanballat, governor of Samaria, and the high priest Johanan, named in 12:22.

context: In the 5th century BC, Judah was a small province of the Persian Empire, with a sparsely populated Jerusalem still without complete walls. Susa, where Nehemiah served, was one of the capitals of the empire. Nehemiah's opponents represented regional forces: Sanballat was linked to the government of Samaria, to the north; Tobiah had connections with the region of Ammon, east of the Jordan; and Geshem led Arab groups of the south, and an inscription on a silver bowl from Egypt mentions a “Geshem, king of Kedar,” perhaps the same person. The crisis of chapter 5 shows the economic difficulties of the province, with debts, mortgages and taxes to the king.
